messages.body_plain:
On Friday, November 22, 2013 12:21:41 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> That should totally go in the manual!

It is in the manual in the subsection on multivariate reparameterizations (p.158). You may have mistakenly looked at the other two places in the Stan manual where multivariate reparameterizations are discussed. But that transformation is more general than just the multivariate normal. A similar thing holds for any elliptical distribution and it is one of the things that we could facilitate with a forward-looking transformation function.

> Could we define a low-rank matrix data type as
> a parameter?

I don't know if it is prevalent enough to be a primitive type. A lot of people fit factor-type models to data or covariance matrices. That is why we needed a Cholesky factor that had more rows than columns so that the rank of  L * L'  is equal to the number of columns of L instead of the number of rows.

Ben

>>> so init=0 does not correspond to sigma=0 but

>> works. Say the first parameter is sigma, and the
>> corresponding init value I give is 1.  Are you saying that means the
>> first value of sigma tried will be e?  I thought
>> the inits, as passed in by me and as returned by get_inits, were on
>> the constrained scale.
>
> Two different things are going on here.
>
> If you take init=0, inits are all 0 on the unconstrained
> scale, and then a parameter sigma constrained to be positive
> will indeed be initialized at 1.
>
> If you take init=2, then inits are uniform at random from [-2,2]
> on the unconstrained scale.
>
> If you specify an init file, they're on the constrained scale.

Are the results of get_inits() on the constrained scale?  If I pass in a
list of values, one per parameter, is that on a constrained scale?  I
was passing in lists.

>
>>> It is always dangerous to throw away initialization a because you
>>> can never tell if there are statistical issues that
>>> are biasing your samples.  Now in practice bad inits in Stan are
>>> usually bad adaptation (as opposed to bad sampling),
>>> so instead
>> My interpretation was that the likelihood could not be evaluated
>> usefully (i.e., either NaN or nothing useful from the
>> derivatives), so that adaptation never got a chance to start. How
>> could adaptation be involved in the failure?
>
> Both things can happen.  You can start in a region where
> Stan gets the gradients right and they're finite, but they're
> so ill conditioned that it'll take a very long time to get to
> the high mass region using our standard adaptation (which
> Michael's working to make better, by the way).
>
> This is arguably an adaptation problem in that what adaptation
> should do is:
>
>   (a) find the high mass region of the posterior,
>
>   (b) estimate the mass (covariance) matrix or an approximation
>       from the high mass region, and
>
>   (c) find a good step sized based on the target acceptance rate.
>
> Any of these can mess up, with the particular problem we usually
> see is (a) being slow and thus biasing (b).
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: rstan permutation paranoia
messages.body_plain:
a <- extract(sf, pars="A")
b <- extract(sf, pars="B")
alist <- extract(sf, pars=c("A", "B"))

In all these cases, can I count on the fact that row i for A (whether
buried in the object a or alist) is from the same chain step as row i
for B (in b or alist)?

The documentation guarantees that
a2 <- extract(sf, pars="A)
will return a2 in the same order as a

The R documentation for extract says "For each ï¿½stanfitï¿½ object, the
permutation is fixed (that is, extracing samples a second
time will give the same sequence of iterations as the
previous)."
which suggests that the permutation is property of the stanfit object,
not the individual parameters, and thus the answer to my question is yes.

A related issue is whether the values for A in a will have the same
ordering as the values for A in alist.

Yes seems like the only reasonable answer to my questions; I just wanted
to double-check.

Ross Boylan

P.S. typo for extrac[t]ing in the quoted documentation.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Trouble initializing with a hierarchical weibull model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Trouble initializing with a hierarchical weibull model
messages.body_plain:
The problem is here:

model {
	vector[N] scale;
	vector[N] shape;
	vector[L] thisScale;
	vector[L] thisShape;
	scalePopMean ~ uniform(4,6);
	shapePopMean ~ uniform(0,2);
	scalePopSD ~ uniform(0,1);
	shapePopSD ~ uniform(0,1);
	scale ~ lognormal(scalePopMean,scalePopSD);
	shape ~ lognormal(shapePopMean,shapePopSD);
	for(i in 1:L){
		thisScale[i] <- scale[unit[i]];
		thisShape[i] <- shape[unit[i]];
	}
	y ~ weibull(thisShape,thisScale);
}

When you call scale ~ lognormal(...) the variable scale is
not set (we default initialize to NaN just to trap errors
like this --- we haven't figured out how to have a good warning
message for using undefined vars yet).

The sampling statements in Stan do not do sampling
per se, they just evaluate the log probability.  If they're unknown,
then you need to make them parameters rather than local variables
in the model.

I'd also add a lower bound to this to check the data's kosher:

	vector[L] y;

should have vector<lower=0>[L] to make sure the data's in range.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, November 25, 2013 12:35:13 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On 11/25/13, 12:32 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> Is there a way we can make what we're doing more robust
> by pivoting.  As you know, my linear algebra fu is weak,
> at best.
>
> It shouldn't be hard to change the behavior, as it's
> a simple function that's already unit tested.

Well, with pivoting it permutes the rows and columns, so it would lead to a lot of user errors. We do use the 3-factor Cholesky with pivoting internally in some case.

Basically, for fixed covariance matrices, you can do the decomposition externally and pass it as data. Or you could do it in Stan via an eigendecomposition instead of the Cholesky decomposition. In the parameterized case, everyone would be better off working with the Cholesky factor primitive types.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Cholesky decomposition with pivoting?
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, November 25, 2013 9:20:02 PM UTC-5, KK Sasa wrote:

> My question is whether I can do the same thing in Stan as in MATLAB when the singular Sigma matrix is parameterized (fixed singular in estimation)?
>
> However, I found that the p. 273 in Stan manual reads
>
> vector eigenvalues_sym(matrix A)
>      The vector of eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix A in descending order
> matrix eigenvectors_sym(matrix A)
>      The matrix with the eigenvectors of symmetric matrix A
>

> The eigenvalues are sorted by default, so does eigenvectors?
> In addition, I found the R function 'eigen' also sorts the eigenvalues in decreasing order, too.

Yes, this method works for any matrix M such that M * M' = A. In this case, M is equal to the matrix of eigenvectors post-multiplied by a diagonal matrix with square roots of eigenvalues, so you have to manually intervene to make sure the last eigenvalue(s) are not slightly negative when they are exactly zero theoretically. You can do it inside Stan that way. The ordering doesn't matter if you are just multiplying by iid standard normals.

Ben

On Tuesday, November 26, 2013 12:11:00 AM UTC-5, KK Sasa wrote:

> The ordering of elements of Sigma is corresponding to my data matrix.

> or boundary conditions in functions (like 0 / 0).

> > error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
> >
> > What general techniques can I use for pinning down the source of my error?
>
> Print results as you go along.
>
> Start with simpler models and build up.  For example,
> build the non-hierarchical version first.
>
> If we had better debuggers, we might not need to
> recommend the first option --- but the second's probably
> good practice for any model-building exercise.
>
>
> > If the model has detected a variable out of range, would it be possible to print the name of this variable and moan
> > about it specifically to help in debugging?
>
> We've been debating how much to intervene with error
> handling.
>
> Right now, we only do thorough checking on the distribution
> functions and some of the other non-built-in functions.
>
> Whatever we do, if we want to get down to checking
> every function including arithmetic operators and
> C++ lib functions like log() and exp(), then we're going to
> need a way to turn it off so there's not too big an efficiency
> hit.  Error checking may seem cheap, but all those branches
> can hurt both inlining at compile time and branch prediction at
> run time.
>
> It's in our sights, but not coming in the very near future.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

   My question is as follows - I had a model where I was modeling observations that lie within the unit interval.  Before, I let these observations come from a normal distribution, which of course isn't accurate since it has support outside the unit interval.  Stan worked well with this model.

   However, I decided to let these observations come from normal distributions truncated to the unit interval (so that I literally only changed 1 line in the model), and now I get the "No acceptably small step size could be found" error.

   Might someone have an intuition on why this might be?  I've tried initializing the parameters from high likelihood locations, but that didn't help.

   I also have a second related question - in general, is there any reason the chain might not move around at all when parameters are initialized at the maximum likelihood location?  I've found that a relatively simple model moves around nicely under random parameter initialization, but doesn't move at all if initialized from maximum likelihood location.

Thanks,
-Fulton

The stan() doc says this for init:

   One of digit 0, string "0" or "random", a function that returns a named list, or
   a list of named list. "0": initialize all to be zero on the unconstrained support;
   "random": randomly generated, see optional parameter init_r; list: a list of lists
   equal in length to the number of chains (parameter chains), where each named list
   (an element of the list of lists) specifies the initial values for parameters by
   names for a chain. function: a function that returns a list for specifying the
   initial values of parameters for a chain. The function can take an optional parameter
   chain_id. See below notes on that RStan treats a vector of length 1 as a scalar

Here is a simple example of the list of named lists approach:

   > fit <- stan('simple.stan',
                 init=list(list(mu=-10000,sigma=10), list(mu=20, sigma=0.1)),
                 chains=2);

Here's an example of using a function:

   > init_fun <- function() { list(mu=runif(1,-1000,1000), sigma=runif(1,0,10)) }

   > fit <- stan('simple.stan', init=init_fun, chains=2)

The doc's a little unclear for someone like me who's not a heavy
R user.  So I created an issue in RStan to update the doc with examples:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/29

- Bob

messages.subject: estimating run time upper limit?
messages.body_plain:
Hi (again) Stan team!

Thanks for all the hard work that went into Stan 2.0, works great!

I do have a question (not specific to 2.0) about timing. The models we are running have large data sets, and take a (very) long time to run. I've been trying to figure out how to determine what sort of runs are realistic in terms of timing, so have am playing with estimating upper bounds for run times. I can time how long it take to evaluate the model block code in the cpp file, and this time seems to be roughly consistent for each step. Then using my maximum tree depth (max_depth), I know the max number of steps per iteration. To compute a run time upper bound, I can then do ub = 2^max_depth*(step_time)*(num_iters) -  assuming that my understanding that the max number of leapfrogs steps per iteration is 2^max_depth is correct. (Similarly for a lower bound.)

The question is whether this is a reasonable way to get an upper bound or do you have ideas of a better way to get at this?

Cheers, and thanks again for all your hard work! Stan is a great tool.

Andria

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] estimating run time upper limit?
messages.body_plain:
On 11/27/13, 4:09 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> max_depth is the depth of the last subtree, so the total number of steps is actually
>
> sum_{i = 0}^{max_depth} 2^{i} \approx 2^{max_depth + 1}

2^0 + ... + 2^N = 2^(N+1) - 1

But this isn't the whole story in terms of number of leapfrog
steps (and hence number of log prob + gradient evals).

The issue is that if NUTS hits a U-turn while constructing
the last subtree, it won't go into the calculation of max depth,
but just be rejected.  That can happen at any point along the
last subtree.  So there's no exact way to recover the number of
evals from the tree depth.

That means the bound you can do from the outside is:

   2^{max_depth + 2} - 1

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
extract is quite slow compared to as.array (13 seconds vs 0.3 s).  I was
a little surprised, and wonder if there's anything that can be done
about it.

OTOH, extract seems to use less space (see Mb for VCells), even though
it's a more complicated structure.  I suppose it must be reusing more of
the stanfit object.

> gc(); system.time(a <- as.array(myfit)); gc()
             used   (Mb) gc trigger   (Mb)  max used   (Mb)

    user  system elapsed
   0.320   0.028   0.347
             used   (Mb) gc trigger   (Mb)  max used   (Mb)
 Ncells   1793322   95.8    2908849  155.4   2908849  155.4
 Vcells 308591810 2354.4  461308458 3519.6 374315795 2855.9
 > class(a)
 [1] "array"
 > dim(a)
 [1] 1500    3 3116
 > gc(); system.time(a <- extract(myfit)); gc()
             used   (Mb) gc trigger   (Mb)  max used   (Mb)
 Ncells   1793316   95.8    2908849  155.4   2908849  155.4
 Vcells 308591801 2354.4  461308458 3519.6 374315795 2855.9
    user  system elapsed
  12.617   0.060  12.718
             used   (Mb) gc trigger   (Mb)  max used   (Mb)
 Ncells   1793451   95.8    4953636  264.6   4953636  264.6
 Vcells 312258836 2382.4  484453880 3696.1 374315795 2855.9
> length(a)
 [1] 18

My interest arises from wanting to do simulations with the values of the
chains, for which I need to extract the coefficients repeatedly.  If I
extract the coefficients each time it will be slow; of course I can
cache the results.  But it would be nice if the values could be accessed
efficiently, e.g., by stanfit[i, j, k] where i is chain, j is step and k
is coefficient.  The grouping of coefficients as in extract may be more
natural for my intended use--I'm not sure what a good interface for that
would be.(*)  Maybe an optional argument j to get just one step of the
chain in extract()...

Ross Boylan

(*) I may be doing out of sample predictions, and so some individual
specific effects will not correspond to any coefficients estimated, but
will need to be drawn from the appropriate hiearchical distn.

messages.body_plain:
On 11/28/13, 2:57 PM, FHRB Toledo wrote:
> Thank you Bob,
>
> In this thread, is there a way to declare casting type within Stan?

I'm not sure what you're asking for.

If you have:

   int n;
   int m;
   double frac;

   frac <- n / m;

then it's probably not going to do what you expect if
your expectations come from R, where "1/4" evaluates to 0.25.
In Stan, "1/4" evaluates to 0.

If you want to force a double-based division on two
integers, you can rely on promotion:

   frac <- n;
   frac <- frac / m;

We don't have any plans to add C-style or C++-style casts.

 > Just to avoid "semantic" errors in the same way as
> in C++ native code!

int / int is defined to return an int, so it's
a feature, not an error, semantic or otherwise.

It absolutely needs to be this way in order to preserve return
types and bottom-up evaluations.  Expressions like "m / n" get evaluated
bottom-up in the sense that they don't depend on the return type.
My understanding is that in R,  everything's underlyingly a double.

- Bob

> On 11/27/13, 6:44 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > Bob's argument is that the last subtree could have gone through almost all of the 2^{depth} iterations before
> > being rejected, and none of those would count because the depth counter wasn't incremented yet.  But that's
> > only a concern if you're trying to determine the number of iterations given some particular value of the the
> > tree depth.
> >
> > max_depth is actually checked before the loop starts, so this concern isn't an issue when determining
> > the largest possible number of iterations.  2^{max_depth + 1} - 1 should be fine.

> Sorry --- Michael's absolutely right, as usual.
> I was mistakenly reading max_depth just as depth.
>
> Most models aren't going to take you anywhere near max_depth,
> and if the tree depths start running up against max_depth and
> there's not a bug in the model, then you probably want to
> increase max_depth.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Nov 27, 2013, at 11:16 PM, Andria Dawson <andria...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >> Hi Bob and Michael,
> >>
> >> Thanks for the quick replies!
> >>
> >> I am still confused about where the additional factor of 2 comes from in the 2^{max_depth + 2} - 1  (i.e. why is it not 2^{max_depth + 1} - 1). If the last subtree is rejected, without having to go into the calculation of max_depth, why is the bound not lower than 2^{max_depth + 1} - 1?
> >>
> >> Thanks!
> >> Andria
> >>
> >> On Wednesday, November 27, 2013 1:25:23 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >>
> >>
> >> On 11/27/13, 4:09 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >>> max_depth is the depth of the last subtree, so the total number of steps is actually
> >>>
> >>> sum_{i = 0}^{max_depth} 2^{i} \approx 2^{max_depth + 1}
> >>
> >> 2^0 + ... + 2^N = 2^(N+1) - 1
> >>
> >> But this isn't the whole story in terms of number of leapfrog
> >> steps (and hence number of log prob + gradient evals).
> >>
> >> The issue is that if NUTS hits a U-turn while constructing
> >> the last subtree, it won't go into the calculation of max depth,
> >> but just be rejected.  That can happen at any point along the
> >> last subtree.  So there's no exact way to recover the number of
> >> evals from the tree depth.
> >>
> >> That means the bound you can do from the outside is:
> >>
> >>     2^{max_depth + 2} - 1
> >>
> >> - Bob

On 11/30/13, 3:06 AM, KK Sasa wrote:

...
 > And I found the definition of dinterval at the webpage
 > <http://jags.sourcearchive.com/documentation/3.1.0/classbugs_1_1DInterval.html>:
 >
 > |
 >
 >   i ~ dinterval(t, cutpoints[])
 >   f(i|t) = 1 if t < cutpoints[i] and t >= cutpoints[i-1]
 >          = 0 otherwise
 >
 > |
 >
 > So, I think I can use custom probability function 'increment_log_prob' in Stan.
 > p. 151 in Stan manual reads it can use increment_log_prob(log(0.0)) to calculate the  log(probability=0).
 > However, I gave it a try, but Stan failed to do this.

If you use increment_log_prob(log(0)), it's equivalent to hard-coding
a sample rejection.  If you initialize at such a state, you'll never
be able to move.

 > Any suggestion for this kind deterministic function?

No.  You shouldn't try to implement dinterval() in Stan.  It's
a hack in JAGS, whereas Stan can just implement the truncation
and censoring models directly.

I'd again urge you to check out the manual chapter on truncation
and censoring.  What you're going to need is a constraint, because
Stan assumes that variables have support (non-zero probability or finite
log probability) on their (possibly constrained) ranges.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
HMC requires derivatives, but we have also taken advantage of autodiff to implement
other algorithms that require derivatives (at the moment mostly optimization algorithms).

The derivatives are of the log posterior with respect to the parameters being sampled
(technical note, actually with parameters mapped into R^{n}, we also automatically
compute the Jacobian and its derivatives as well).

Depending on your problem you should be able to map the derivatives to their
Laplace equivalents and invert each element of the gradient to get reasonably
efficient analytic gradients, but it would be difficult to embed that into Stan given that
our code does not allow custom gradient evaluations.
